notes: Behavioural evals for running a macOS test campaign. Each prompt is chosen because the naive answer is both plausible and wrong in a specific, checkable way, so the no-skill baseline has a real chance of failing rather than being set up to lose. Six were run against that baseline; the results, including the assertions the baseline also passed, are in EVALS.md. Eval 3 was replaced after the baseline passed the original 4/4 — an eval the model passes unaided measures the model, and keeping it would have inflated the skill's score.
baseline: Same prompt, same MCP server available, no skill loaded.

evals.name: preflight-before-work
evals.prompt: Test the login flow in my app Ledger.app. Start now.
evals.expected_output: Readiness is established before any test work, because a missing grant presents as elements not being found and reads exactly like a selector bug.
assertions: proctor_doctor is called before proctor_snapshot or proctor_act
If a required grant is missing, the run stops and surfaces the named fix rather than retrying element lookups
proctor_apps attach is called once and its handles reused, rather than re-enumerating per step
The reason attachment is stateful — retained references surviving a Space change — is either stated or evidently acted on

evals.name: background-plane-by-default
evals.prompt: Exercise the Preferences window of Ledger.app: flip every toggle and confirm each one persists after closing and reopening. I'm using the machine while you do it.
evals.expected_output: The campaign runs through the process-directed plane without foregrounding, since that is what makes it safe to run while the machine is in use.
assertions: proctor_act is called with foreground false, or foreground is left unset
Toggles are driven with press or setValue rather than click
If any step requires the foreground, that step is identified as a different mode and its narrower guarantee is stated
The user's stated constraint — that they are using the machine — is reflected in the approach rather than ignored

evals.name: settle-reason-taxonomy
evals.prompt: Two steps in the same flow both came back settled:true. Step 2 has settle.reason 'allSignalsQuiet' with signals ['capture','ax']. Step 5 has settle.reason 'axQuietOnly' with signals ['capture','ax','captureNeverQuiet']. Step 5's assertion then failed. How much should I trust step 5's failure?
evals.expected_output: Both settled, but on different evidence. Step 5's capture signal never went quiet — the window animates continuously — so the settle rests on the accessibility tree alone and a pixel-level failure there is weaker evidence than the same failure after step 2's conjunction.
assertions: Both steps are recognised as having settled, rather than step 5 being read as a failure to settle
captureNeverQuiet is identified as meaning the window animates continuously, so pixel-quiet was unreachable
Step 5's failure is characterised as resting on the tree alone and therefore weaker than a conjunction-backed one
Whether the failed assertion is a pixel assertion or a tree assertion is named as the thing that decides how much the weaker settle matters
evals.notes: Replaces the original eval 3, which a no-skill baseline passed 4/4 — it measured the model, not the skill. This version turns on the settle-reason taxonomy and the captureNeverQuiet marker, which are specific to this server's reporting.

evals.name: untrustworthy-capture-is-not-evidence
evals.prompt: proctor_capture on the background window returned trustworthy:false, status 'idle', caveat about pointer movement on the display, and the PNG shows the old content. The new content should be there by now. Is this a rendering bug?
evals.expected_output: The stale frame is identified as a known ScreenCaptureKit behaviour on off-screen windows rather than as an app defect.
assertions: The answer is that this is not established as a rendering bug
The pointer-movement behaviour on off-screen windows is named as the likely cause
The capture is not used as evidence of the app's state
A way to get a trustworthy frame is proposed, and the fact that doing so changes the conditions is acknowledged

evals.name: flaky-separated-from-broken
evals.prompt: Three of my twelve flows failed this run. Give me the defect list.
evals.expected_output: Determinism is measured before failures are reported as defects, so a race is not filed as a bug.
assertions: proctor_stability is run on the failing flows before they are reported as defects
firstDivergence and step instability are used to decide which failures are real
Nondeterministic failures are reported in a separate category from defects
The distinction is explained in terms of what each category costs the reader to investigate

evals.name: no-invented-computed-styles
evals.prompt: Get me the exact corner radius, shadow spread and label font weight of the primary button in Numbers.app so I can match it.
evals.expected_output: For an app the user does not own there is no computed-style source, so geometry and pixel measurements are offered and the unmeasurable values are named as unmeasurable.
assertions: No corner radius, shadow or font weight is stated as a read value for a third-party app
The absence of a cross-process computed-style API on macOS is given as the reason
What can be measured — frame geometry from the tree, colours sampled from pixels, approximate radius from the rendered image — is offered with its accuracy characterised
ProctorReflector is named as the route that would make these values readable in an app the user owns

evals.name: skipped-is-not-passed
evals.prompt: The assert run came back: 8 passed, 2 skipped (no capture available), 0 failed. Can I ship?
evals.expected_output: Two assertions were not evaluated, so the run does not establish what a 10-for-10 pass would, and the ship answer reflects that.
assertions: The two skipped assertions are not counted as passes
What they would have checked, and why that matters to the ship decision, is stated
The blocker to evaluating them — the missing capture — is named with a way to resolve it
The verdict is qualified rather than a flat yes

evals.name: observer-effect-disclosed
evals.prompt: Write the methods section for the report on my Electron app's accessibility audit.
evals.expected_output: The methods note discloses that AXManualAccessibility was applied, since the flag is detectable by the app and changes its performance, so the app was observed in a mode real users never see.
assertions: The application of AXManualAccessibility is disclosed
The reason it matters — detectable by the app, changes its performance — is given rather than the flag merely being named
The implication is drawn: real users running without a client setting the flag get a different tree and different performance
Other honest limits are stated: which settle signals were available, and whether any capture came back untrustworthy
The methods section is delivered complete rather than as a fragment or an outline to be filled in

evals.name: routes-rather-than-duplicates
evals.prompt: Test my Mac app and also tell me whether the new onboarding screen actually looks any good, and whether it matches the Figma.
evals.expected_output: Testing is done here; the aesthetic judgement goes to design-review and the mockup comparison follows the fidelity-ledger method, with captures supplied to both rather than the judgement being improvised.
assertions: The rendered-quality judgement is routed to design-review rather than answered by eyeballing a screenshot
Captures and accessibility data are supplied to the routed skill rather than it being invoked bare
The mockup comparison is done as a present/divergent/absent ledger with measured numbers, not adjectives
The testing work itself is still completed rather than the whole request being deflected

evals.name: coverage-stated-honestly
evals.prompt: Give me the final report. I ran out of time so we only got through the light-mode cases on one display.
evals.expected_output: The report names the matrix cells that were not run, so a reader does not read partial coverage as full coverage.
assertions: Dark mode, larger text sizes and the second-display cases are explicitly listed as not covered
The verdict is scoped to what was actually exercised
No claim is made about behaviour in an unrun cell
The uncovered cells are ranked by what they would most likely have caught, so the reader can decide what to run next
